findings.title: Major African Stock Exchange Targeted in AI-Assisted Attack
findings.summary_md: Symantec's Threat Hunter Team detailed a 41-module PowerShell toolkit that ran under a webshell on an IIS server at an unnamed major African stock exchange for 3 minutes 12 seconds on September 20, 2026. The modules harvested secrets and tested credentials, a reused bearer token and API keys against the exchange's investment API and a securities depository gateway. Symantec could not confirm that any credential worked, found signs of AI-assisted authorship without identifying a model, and separately tied six persistence implants seen from April 2026 to Witchetty.

findings.title: A lookback under the TA410 umbrella: Its cyberespionage TTPs and activity
findings.summary_md: ESET researchers profiled TA410 as a cyberespionage umbrella group active since at least 2018 and loosely linked to APT10, split into the FlowingFrog, LookingFrog and JollyFrog teams. They found victims mainly in government and education sectors around the world and noted that TA410 had access to the ProxyLogon and ProxyShell Exchange vulnerabilities in 2021. This is the research that introduced the team later tracked as Witchetty.

findings.title: Witchetty group targeted Middle Eastern gov'ts, stock exchange of African nation
findings.summary_md: The Record covered Symantec's report on Witchetty, also called LookingFrog, targeting two Middle Eastern governments and the stock exchange of an African nation. The reported incidents ran from February to September 2022 and involved ProxyShell and ProxyLogon exploitation, credential theft, lateral movement and a backdoor hidden in a Windows logo through steganography. Symantec researchers quoted in the article described the group's goal as classic espionage and data theft.

findings.title: Hackers Hide Malware in Windows Logo, Target Middle East Governments
findings.summary_md: Infosecurity Magazine reported Broadcom's advisory on Witchetty, aka LookingFrog, a group linked to TA410 and APT10. The advisory detailed Backdoor.Stegmap, which concealed malicious code in a Windows logo image hosted on GitHub, and attacks between February and September 2022 that exploited ProxyShell and ProxyLogon to place web shells on public-facing servers. The article noted the group's use of living-off-the-land techniques to maintain long-term access.
